sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Xerocomellus chrysenteron has a dry grey-brown to olive-brown cap, often cracking in dry weather to reveal pink-red flesh. The tubes are yellow then olive-yellow, with wide angular pores that bruise blue only weakly or slowly. The slender yellow stem often has red fibrils or dots, especially towards the base.

sections.title: Cut surface and useful characters
sections.text: The cap flesh is whitish to yellowish. Stem flesh remains cream to yellow, sometimes red beneath the surface or near the base; it does not turn uniformly beetroot red. The spore print is olive-brown. Bluing is weak or absent, and close relatives may require microscopic examination.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: The species is often found under conifers, but also near beech and other broad-leaved trees. It fruits from summer to autumn, sometimes into November.

sections.title: Lookalikes and safety
sections.text: Xerocomellus cisalpinus and other small cracked boletes can look similar; stem-base flesh colour helps but is not always conclusive. DGfM and VAPKO list it as edible; references recommend thorough cooking and describe its culinary quality as modest. Eat only specimens identified with certainty.

traits: Grey-brown to olive-brown cap, 3 to 8 cm, dry, quickly cracking to show pink-red flesh in the cracks
Yellow then olive-yellow tubes; wide, angular pores that hardly turn blue
Slender yellow stem, often marked with red fibrils, especially near the base
Cream to yellow flesh, sometimes red beneath the basal surface; it does not turn uniformly red when cut
Often under conifers, sometimes near beech and other broad-leaved trees · summer to autumn
safetyNote: Listed as edible by DGfM and VAPKO, but of modest culinary quality and requiring thorough cooking. Several close relatives are difficult to distinguish; have the identification checked.
